<reason>B established the stronger comparative case: recognition creates an additional accountability route without requiring universal enforcement. Its dam answer supplied concrete evidence of unnecessary destruction, rather than abandoning the proposed standard as A alleged. A raised substantial predictability and selective-enforcement concerns, but overstated them into inevitable arbitrariness and uselessness. Its redundancy argument also failed to distinguish existing domestic offenses from accountability beyond a protecting government. B answered the central pressure more directly and maintained better-qualified claims.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s strongest rebuttal distinguished an unwilling host government from a willing arrest state. This directly undermined A’s claim that the backstop works only where domestic prosecution already functions. A’s travel-avoidance response limited likely enforcement but did not eliminate the additional route B defended.</best_rebuttal>
